question:
Consider the following statements about the Dalhousie period.

1. The first railway line in India from Bombay to Thane was opened in 1853.

2. The Post Office Act of 1854 introduced postage stamps in India.

3. Civil services were opened to competitive examination under the Charter Act of 1833.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the first railway line, from Bombay to Thane (about 34 km), was opened on 16 April 1853 during Dalhousie's term (डलहौजी काल — रेल, डाक और तार)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the Post Office Act of 1854 reorganised the postal service on a uniform rate and introduced postage stamps for the first time.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong: competitive examinations for the civil services were initiated through the Charter Act of 1853, in Dalhousie's period, and not the Act of 1833.

 

• The electric telegraph line from Calcutta to Agra was established in 1853-54, and a separate Public Works Department was created.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Dalhousie's railway minute of 1853 sketched the main trunk lines connecting Bombay, Calcutta and Madras.

 

• The Charter Act of 1853 ended the Company's patronage in appointments to the civil service.

 

• Lord Macaulay chaired the committee of 1854 that framed the rules for open competition.

 

• The telegraph was developed by William O'Shaughnessy.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 1): Selecting 1 and 3 only accepts the wrong date for the civil service competition, which began with the Act of 1853; it also leaves out the Post Office Act that brought postage stamps.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 2): Opting for 2 and 3 only drops the true statement about the first railway line of 1853 and takes the competitive-examination claim, whose Act of 1833 attribution is erroneous.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Including all three statements fails because the competitive examination was introduced under the Charter Act of 1853 and not 1833; the Act of 1833 only opened offices to all in principle.

question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order.

1. Opening of the Bombay-Thane railway line

2. Annexation of Satara by the Doctrine of Lapse

3. Wood's Educational Despatch

4. Outbreak of the Revolt of 1857
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2-1-3-4.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The first annexation under the Doctrine of Lapse, Satara, took place in 1848, so event 2 comes first (डलहौजी काल की घटनाओं का कालक्रम)

 

• The Bombay-Thane railway opened on 16 April 1853, which makes event 1 the second event.

 

• Wood's Despatch of 1854, called the Intellectual Charter of India, follows next as event 3.

 

• The Revolt of 1857 broke out on 10 May at Meerut and closes the sequence, giving the order 2-1-3-4.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Wood's Despatch recommended a hierarchy of schools, universities at the presidency capitals and grants-in-aid.

 

• The universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were founded in 1857.

 

• Dalhousie left India in 1856, so the Revolt took place under Canning.

 

• Annexation of Awadh (1856) was the last major annexation before the Revolt.

 

NOTE

 

• 1-2-3-4 (Option 1): This order puts the railway before Satara, but the Satara annexation took place in 1848, five years before the first train ran from Bombay to Thane in 1853.

 

• 2-3-1-4 (Option 2): This order sets Wood's Despatch (1854) ahead of the railway (1853), reversing the actual sequence by one year; the railway line was formally opened in April 1853.

 

• 2-1-4-3 (Option 4): This order places the Revolt of 1857 ahead of Wood's Despatch, which was issued in 1854; the Revolt began three years later and so must be the final event in the list.

question:
Match the following with the year to which they relate.

Column A: (a) Wood's Despatch (b) English Education Act (c) Indian Universities Act (d) Foundation of the Universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras

Column B: (i) 1835 (ii) 1854 (iii) 1857 (iv) 1904
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• (a) Wood's Despatch was issued in 1854 under Dalhousie and is called the Intellectual Charter of India, so a-ii (शिक्षा संबंधी अधिनियम और उनके वर्ष)

 

• (b) The English Education Act was passed in 1835 under Bentinck, following Macaulay's Minute, so b-i.

 

• (c) The Indian Universities Act was enacted in 1904 by Curzon after the Raleigh Commission, so c-iv.

 

• (d) The first universities at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were founded in 1857, so d-iii.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Wood's Despatch recommended universities modelled on London University.

 

• The Raleigh Commission of 1902 examined the state of universities.

 

• Curzon's Act of 1904 gave universities greater control over affiliated colleges and tightened government control.

 

• The Hunter Commission of 1882 dealt with primary and secondary education.

 

• Macaulay's Minute of 1835 had championed English instruction, whereas Wood's Despatch of 1854 promoted vernacular schools at the lower level.

 

NOTE

 

• a-i, b-ii, c-iv, d-iii (Option 1): This combination swaps the first two years; Wood's Despatch dates to 1854 and the English Education Act to 1835, so assigning 1835 to the Despatch and 1854 to the Act is incorrect.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv (Option 3): This combination reverses the last two years, giving 1857 to the Indian Universities Act and 1904 to the three presidency universities, whereas the Act belongs to Curzon's 1904 and the universities to 1857.

 

• a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i (Option 4): This combination reverses the whole list, giving 1904 to Wood's Despatch and 1835 to the foundation of the universities, so every pair is misplaced and none of the dates matches.

question: Who was the last Governor-General and the first Viceroy of India, during whose tenure the Revolt of 1857 took place?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Canning.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lord Canning (1856-62) was the last Governor-General of India and, after the Government of India Act 1858, the first Viceroy (लॉर्ड कैनिंग — अंतिम गवर्नर-जनरल और प्रथम वायसराय)

 

• The Revolt of 1857 broke out in his tenure, and Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1 November 1858, announced by him at Allahabad, transferred authority from the Company to the Crown.

 

• The Proclamation promised respect for the rights of princes, religious tolerance and an end to annexation, leading to the withdrawal of the Doctrine of Lapse.

 

• He also oversaw the passing of the Indian Councils Act 1861, which began association of Indians with legislation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The title Viceroy denoted the Crown's representative, while the Governor-General remained the official head of administration.

 

• The Secretary of State for India with a Council of India replaced the Board of Control.

 

• The Indian High Courts Act of 1861 set up High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras.

 

• Canning is said to have earned the nickname 'Clemency Canning' for his moderation in 1857.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Dalhousie (Option 1): Lord Dalhousie left office in March 1856 just before the Revolt and served only as Governor-General; he never held the title of Viceroy, which was created after the Crown took charge in 1858.

 

• Lord Elgin I (Option 2): Lord Elgin I (1862-63) succeeded Canning as the second Viceroy and died at Dharamsala in 1863; he did not hold office at the time of the Revolt of 1857.

 

• Lord Mayo (Option 4): Lord Mayo became Viceroy in 1869, twelve years after the Revolt, and was assassinated in 1872 at Port Blair; he was neither the first Viceroy nor in office in 1857.

question:
Consider the following statements about the period of Lord Canning.

1. The Doctrine of Lapse was abandoned after the Revolt of 1857.

2. The Widow Remarriage Act was passed in 1856 through the efforts of Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.

3. The Ilbert Bill was introduced in his tenure.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: following the Revolt, the policy of annexation was dropped and the Doctrine of Lapse was abolished, with the Proclamation of 1858 guaranteeing the right of adoption (कैनिंग काल की घटनाएँ)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (1856), drafted in Dalhousie's time, was passed under Canning through the efforts of Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong because the Ilbert Bill (1883) belongs to the Viceroyalty of Lord Ripon, more than two decades later.

 

• Canning's tenure also saw the Indian Penal Code (1860) and the first Indian budget presented by James Wilson.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Vidyasagar petitioned the government with nearly 1000 signatures in support of widow remarriage.

 

• C. P. Ilbert was the Law Member who introduced the bill that was named after him.

 

• The Doctrine of Lapse had earlier been used by Dalhousie in Satara and Nagpur.

 

• Canning's term saw the establishment of the Universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras in 1857.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 1): Going with 1 and 3 only denies the Widow Remarriage Act of 1856 and relies on the Ilbert Bill, which was connected to Ripon in 1883 and was not a measure of Canning's tenure.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): Choosing 2 and 3 only omits the abandonment of the Doctrine of Lapse after the Revolt, while accepting the Ilbert Bill, which pertains to the Ripon years (1880-84) rather than Canning's.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Accepting all three is wrong because the Ilbert Bill of 1883 was linked with Lord Ripon, two Viceroys' terms later than Canning; it was proposed by Law Member C. P. Ilbert.

question:
Match the Viceroy in Column A with the event in Column B.

Column A: (a) Lord Canning (b) Lord Mayo (c) Lord Lytton (d) Lord Ripon

Column B: (i) Local self-government resolution (ii) First Census of India (iii) Vernacular Press Act (iv) Indian Penal Code
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• (a) Under Canning, the Indian Penal Code was passed in 1860, so a-iv (वायसराय और उनके कार्य — मिलान)

 

• (b) The first Census of India was conducted in 1872 under Lord Mayo, so b-ii.

 

• (c) Lord Lytton passed the Vernacular Press Act in 1878, so c-iii.

 

• (d) Lord Ripon passed the resolution on local self-government in 1882, so d-i.

 

• These four measures cover Canning's legal code, Mayo's statistical record keeping, Lytton's curbs on Indian-language papers and Ripon's plan for elected local boards, which fixes the correct pairing as a-iv, b-ii, c-iii and d-i.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Macaulay drafted the IPC in the 1830s as head of the Law Commission.

 

• Regular decennial census began in 1881 under Ripon.

 

• Lytton's Act was repealed in 1882.

 

• Ripon's Resolution gave elected non-official majorities in local boards.

 

• Lord Ripon's Resolution is frequently cited as the starting point of democratic institutions at the grassroots level in British India.

 

• The Indian Penal Code was drafted by the first Law Commission headed by Macaulay, passed in 1860 and brought into operation on 1 January 1862.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i (Option 1): This combination swaps the Mayo and Lytton events, but the census of 1872 belonged to Mayo and the Vernacular Press Act to Lytton, so b-iii and c-ii are both incorrect.

 

• a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i (Option 2): This combination mixes up the first two rows, giving the census to Canning and the IPC to Mayo, while Canning's IPC came into force in 1860 and Mayo's census in 1872.

 

• a-iv, b-i, c-iii, d-ii (Option 4): This combination gives the local self-government resolution to Mayo and the first Census to Ripon; only the Canning and Lytton entries are correct, because Mayo held the 1872 census and Ripon the resolution.

question:
Consider the following statements about Lord Mayo.

1. He introduced the financial decentralisation between the central and provincial governments.

2. The Statistical Survey of India was established during his tenure.

3. The Vernacular Press Act was passed during his tenure.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Mayo's resolution of 1870 started financial decentralisation, giving provincial governments fixed grants for subjects such as police, jails and education (मेयो — वित्तीय विकेंद्रीकरण 1870)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the Statistical Survey of India was established in his tenure, and he also initiated jail reforms.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong because the Vernacular Press Act (1878) was passed by Lord Lytton, six years after Mayo's death.

 

• Mayo died in 1872, and the census of that year is also connected to his term.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mayo founded Mayo College at Ajmer for the education of princes.

 

• He created the Department of Agriculture and Commerce in 1871.

 

• Mayo was the only Viceroy to be killed in office, by Sher Ali Afridi at Port Blair.

 

• Provincial finance was further widened by Lytton in 1877.

 

• Mayo's tenure from 1869 to 1872 was ended by his murder while he was inspecting the Andaman penal settlement.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): Selecting 1 and 3 only credits Mayo with the press law, which was Lytton's work of 1878, and it overlooks the Statistical Survey set up during Mayo's own tenure.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): Opting for 2 and 3 only ignores the decentralisation of finance in 1870 and accepts the Vernacular Press Act, which was not enacted until 1878 under Lytton.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Taking all three statements is wrong because the Vernacular Press Act was a Lytton measure of 1878, while the other two statements concern real administrative steps of the Mayo period.

question: Which Viceroy was assassinated at Port Blair in the Andaman Islands in 1872 by the convict Sher Ali Afridi?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Mayo.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lord Mayo (Viceroy 1869-72) was stabbed to death in 1872 by Sher Ali Afridi during a visit to the Andamans, the only Viceroy to be assassinated in India (लॉर्ड मेयो की हत्या — पोर्ट ब्लेयर, 1872)

 

• Sher Ali Afridi, a Pathan convict, attacked him as he returned to his ship after inspecting the convict settlement.

 

• Mayo's financial reforms and the Mayo College at Ajmer are remembered as lasting contributions.

 

• He was succeeded by Lord Northbrook (1872-76).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The first census of India was taken in 1872 during Mayo's rule.

 

• The Wahabi trials and the killing of Chief Justice Norman in 1871 preceded this attack.

 

• Elgin I died of illness at Dharamsala in 1863.

 

• The Andaman penal settlement had been set up after the Revolt of 1857.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Lytton (Option 1): Lord Lytton served through 1876-80 and survived his term, returning to Europe afterwards; he is known for the Vernacular Press Act and the Second Afghan War rather than assassination.

 

• Lord Northbrook (Option 2): Lord Northbrook succeeded Mayo after the murder and finished his term in 1876 without being attacked; he is linked with the Bengal famine relief of 1873-74.

 

• Lord Elgin I (Option 3): Lord Elgin I (1862-63) died of a heart attack on a tour at Dharamsala; his death was natural and occurred a decade before the Port Blair incident.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Arms Act (1878) of Lord Lytton.

1. A licence became mandatory to keep arms.

2. Europeans and Anglo-Indians were exempted from its provisions.

3. The Act was passed for the purpose of encouraging Indians to bear arms against foreign enemies.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Arms Act (1878) made it compulsory to hold a licence for keeping arms (लिटन का शस्त्र अधिनियम 1878)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: Europeans and Anglo-Indians were exempt, which made the law a racially discriminatory measure.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong because the Act disarmed Indians and discouraged arms ownership, and it did not promote military recruitment against foreign enemies.

 

• The Act, along with the Vernacular Press Act of the same year, fed the resentment that later contributed to the rise of the Indian National Congress.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Vernacular Press Act (1878) authorised the confiscation of newspaper property if a bond was violated.

 

• The Delhi Durbar of 1877 proclaimed Queen Victoria Kaiser-i-Hind.

 

• Lytton's Statutory Civil Service scheme of 1879 reserved a minority of posts for Indians of high birth.

 

• Together with the Vernacular Press Act, the Arms Act made the Lytton years among the most disliked of the period.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 1): Going with 1 and 3 only treats the Act as a measure to encourage arming Indians, which is the reverse of its intent, and it ignores the exemption of Europeans and Anglo-Indians.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 2): Choosing 2 and 3 only drops the licence requirement, the basic provision of the Act, and falls for the false claim that the Act encouraged Indians to arm themselves.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): All three cannot be right because the third statement misstates the Act's purpose; the law restricted arms for Indians through licences while exempting Europeans, and it did not recruit anyone.

question: The Second Anglo-Afghan War (1878-80), fought during the Viceroyalty of Lord Lytton, ended with which treaty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Treaty of Gandamak.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Treaty of Gandamak (1879) was signed with Yakub Khan, the Amir of Afghanistan, ending the first phase of the Second Anglo-Afghan War under Lytton (गंदमक की संधि — द्वितीय अफगान युद्ध)

 

• By it Afghanistan accepted a British Resident at Kabul, handed over control of foreign relations and ceded border districts such as the Khyber and Michni passes.

 

• The British Resident Cavagnari was killed at Kabul soon after, and fighting resumed.

 

• The war was a result of Lytton's Forward Policy, aimed at countering Russian influence in Afghanistan.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Lytton's term also had the Great Famine of 1876-78.

 

• He made Queen Victoria Empress of India at the Delhi Durbar of 1877.

 

• The war ended finally with the recognition of Abdur Rahman as Amir.

 

• Lytton resigned with the fall of Disraeli's government in 1880.

 

• Yakub Khan became Amir after Sher Ali's death, and he signed the treaty under heavy British military pressure in May 1879.

 

NOTE

 

• Treaty of Lahore (Option 2): The Treaty of Lahore was signed in 1846 after the First Anglo-Sikh War between the Sikh Empire and the Company, so it belongs to the Hardinge I period and not to Afghanistan.

 

• Treaty of Srirangapatam (Option 3): The Treaty of Srirangapatam (1792) concluded the Third Anglo-Mysore War under Cornwallis and had nothing to do with Afghanistan or the later nineteenth century.

 

• Treaty of Salbai (Option 4): The Treaty of Salbai (1782) ended the First Anglo-Maratha War during Warren Hastings's period; it is a Maratha settlement and belongs to a century earlier than Lytton.

question: By how much did Lord Lytton reduce the maximum age for appearing in the Indian Civil Service examination, a step that reduced the chances of Indian candidates?
solution_text:
The correct answer is From 21 to 19 years.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lytton lowered the maximum age for the ICS examination from 21 to 19 years, making it very difficult for Indians to travel to London and compete (लिटन — आईसीएस परीक्षा की अधिकतम आयु 21 से 19)

 

• The ICS examination was held only in London, and the lower age limit was a way of denying Indians a fair chance despite the Act of 1853.

 

• The measure produced strong protests, and Surendranath Banerjee, who had been disqualified on a technicality, toured India in 1877 against the injustice.

 

• The grievance became one of the issues around which the Indian Association (1876) rallied public opinion.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Satyendranath Tagore (1863) was the first Indian to join the ICS.

 

• Indian candidates were permitted to sit the examination in India simultaneously only after 1922.

 

• Lytton's Statutory Civil Service of 1878-79 offered a small number of posts to Indians of good families.

 

• Surendranath Banerjee later founded the Indian Association.

 

NOTE

 

• From 23 to 21 years (Option 1): The range from 23 to 21 years does not match the change; the earlier limit was 21, and it was cut to 19, so the starting point in this option is incorrect.

 

• From 25 to 22 years (Option 3): The range from 25 to 22 years is wrong because the limit was never 25 under Lytton; the actual lowering took the limit down by two years to 19 and not by three.

 

• From 21 to 17 years (Option 4): The range from 21 to 17 years begins correctly at 21 but overstates the reduction; Lytton brought it down to 19 and not to 17, which would have excluded nearly every candidate.

question:
Assertion (A): Lord Ripon is called the Father of Local Self-Government in India.

Reason (R): His resolution of 1882 provided for elected local bodies such as municipal bodies and panchayats.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: A is true but R is false
option_3: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Assertion A is true: Lord Ripon (1880-84) is known as the Father of Local Self-Government in India (रिपन — स्थानीय स्वशासन के जनक)

 

• Reason R is also true: his Resolution of 1882 envisaged local boards and municipal bodies with a majority of elected non-official members.

 

• The reason explains the assertion because the 1882 scheme was the first real step towards elected local bodies in India, which is why Ripon is given the title.

 

• The scheme did not work fully in practice because officials kept control over the bodies' chairmanship and finance.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ripon repealed the Vernacular Press Act in 1882.

 

• The first Indian Factory Act of 1881 was passed under him.

 

• He is also called the Father of the Indian Census because regular census began in 1881.

 

• Ripon's popularity among Indians was unmatched among Viceroys, and he was feted in 1884.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): The second option accepts the statements but denies the connection; the 1882 Resolution on local bodies is the very measure for which Ripon earned the title, so it directly explains the assertion.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 2): The third option calls the Reason false, but the Resolution of 1882 did provide for municipal and rural local bodies with elected non-official members, as noted in the standard accounts.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): The fourth option calls the Assertion false, but Ripon is widely called the Father of Local Self-Government in India, and the description is a standard textbook fact.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Ilbert Bill controversy.

1. The Bill was introduced in 1883 during the Viceroyalty of Lord Ripon.

2. It aimed to allow Indian judges to try Europeans.

3. It was passed by the Government in its original form without any change.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Ilbert Bill (1883), named after the Law Member C. P. Ilbert, was introduced under Lord Ripon (इल्बर्ट बिल विवाद 1883)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the Bill sought to end the racial discrimination in the Criminal Procedure Code that prevented Indian judges and magistrates from trying European offenders.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong because the strong opposition of Europeans, the 'White Mutiny', forced the government to compromise; a modified version was passed in 1884 giving Europeans the right to be tried by a jury with a majority of Europeans.

 

• The affair showed Indians that racial prejudice was strong and boosted political consciousness before the Indian National Congress was formed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Surendranath Banerjee was jailed in 1883 for contempt of court, which provoked widespread protests.

 

• Ripon left India in 1884 after the controversy.

 

• The Bill was brought to extend the powers of Indian civil servants such as Behari Lal Gupta.

 

• Congress was founded in 1885, soon after this episode.

 

• Ripon came to India as Gladstone's nominee, and his sympathy for Indians angered the European community in Calcutta.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 1): Selecting 1 and 3 only treats the Bill as passed unchanged, but the compromise of 1884 diluted it by allowing European accused a jury of which at least half were Europeans.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): Opting for 2 and 3 only drops the correct date and Viceroy information, and mistakenly accepts that the Bill passed in unaltered form after European protests.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Taking all three statements is wrong; although the first two are accurate, the Bill was watered down in 1884 by a compromise, so it was not accepted in its original shape.

question: The Hunter Commission (1882), appointed under Lord Ripon, was set up to review the progress of
option_4: Elementary and secondary education in British India
solution_text:
The correct answer is Elementary and secondary education in British India.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Hunter Commission (1882), headed by Sir William Hunter, was appointed to investigate the non-implementation of Wood's Despatch of 1854 and to assess elementary and secondary education (हंटर आयोग 1882 — शिक्षा की समीक्षा)

 

• It emphasised primary education, recommending that it be transferred to the control of district and municipal boards and that private effort be encouraged in secondary education.

 

• It advised the government to withdraw gradually from direct management of higher education.

 

• It was set up under Ripon, who is regarded as a liberal Viceroy sympathetic to Indian demands.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Raleigh Commission (1902) reviewed universities under Curzon.

 

• The Sadler Commission (1917-19) studied Calcutta University.

 

• Famine commissions were appointed under Lytton (Strachey Commission, 1880) and Elgin II (Lyall Commission, 1898).

 

• Ripon's Resolution on local self-government paired with the commission's primary school proposal.

 

• Commission members included Indian representatives such as Syed Mahmud, Bhudev Mukherjee and Anandamohan Bose, besides European officials.

 

NOTE

 

• Famine relief measures (Option 1): Famine relief was the subject of the Strachey Famine Commission (1880) under Lytton and the Lyall Commission (1898) under Elgin II; the Hunter Commission had an educational charge and not a famine one.

 

• Police administration (Option 2): Police administration was reviewed by the Fraser Commission of 1902 under Curzon; the Hunter Commission of 1882 had no remit over police matters.

 

• Revenue settlement (Option 3): Revenue settlement was the topic of land-tax debates and of Curzon's resolution of 1902; the Hunter Commission was set up for education, so a revenue charge is incorrect.

question: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 by A. O. Hume during the Viceroyalty of
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Dufferin.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lord Dufferin (1884-88) was the Viceroy when the Indian National Congress was founded in December 1885 at Bombay by A. O. Hume (कांग्रेस की स्थापना 1885 — डफरिन)

 

• The first session was presided over by W. C. Bonnerjee and was attended by 72 delegates.

 

• Dufferin is said to have encouraged Hume to form an organisation to provide a safety-valve for discontent, although later he became hostile to the Congress.

 

• His term included the annexation of Upper Burma (1886) after the Third Anglo-Burmese War.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ripon (1880-84) preceded Dufferin, and Lansdowne (1888-94) followed him.

 

• Hume was a retired civil servant of the Indian Civil Service.

 

• The Congress held its second session at Calcutta in 1886 under Dadabhai Naoroji.

 

• Curzon's term (1899-1905) saw the Partition of Bengal.

 

• The Congress's early demands included Indianisation of the services, expansion of the legislative councils and reduction of military expenditure.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Ripon (Option 1): Lord Ripon left India in 1884, a year before the Congress was founded, and is known instead for local self-government and the Ilbert Bill controversy; he was no longer Viceroy in 1885.

 

• Lord Lansdowne (Option 2): Lord Lansdowne became Viceroy in 1888, three years after the Congress had been founded, and he passed the Indian Councils Act of 1892 as a response to its demands.

 

• Lord Curzon (Option 4): Lord Curzon took charge in 1899, fourteen years after the founding of the Congress, and is remembered for the Partition of Bengal of 1905 and the Universities Act of 1904.

question:
Assertion (A): The Indian Councils Act of 1892, passed under Lord Lansdowne, introduced the principle of indirect election for the first time.

Reason (R): The Act provided that members of the Legislative Councils were to be directly elected by the general voters.
option_1: A is true but R is false
option_2: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_3: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is A is true but R is false.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Assertion A is true: the Indian Councils Act 1892, passed in the Viceroyalty of Lord Lansdowne (1888-94), brought in indirect election for the first time (भारतीय परिषद अधिनियम 1892 — अप्रत्यक्ष चुनाव)

 

• Reason R is false because there was no direct voting by the public; non-official members were nominated by the Governor-General or Governors on the recommendation of bodies like universities, municipalities, district boards and chambers of commerce.

 

• The Act also enlarged the councils and gave members the right to discuss the budget and to put questions, though not to vote or ask supplementary questions.

 

• The word 'election' itself was avoided in the Act, as the recommended persons were formally nominated.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Indian Councils Act of 1861 first allowed non-official Indian nominations.

 

• Direct elections became part of the system through the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms of 1919.

 

• Lansdowne's term also had the Durand Line agreement (1893) with Afghanistan.

 

• The Age of Consent Act (1891) was passed during Lansdowne's period.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A (Option 2): The second option claims that both statements are true and linked, but the Reason fails because the council members were recommended by institutions and nominated; direct election by the public came only later.

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 3): The third option treats the Reason as a true fact; however, it describes an electoral process that did not exist in 1892, so the Reason cannot even be accepted as true.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): The fourth option denies the Assertion, but the 1892 Act is widely cited as the first instance of indirect election in the Indian constitutional development, so the Assertion is true.

question: W. C. Rand, the Plague Commissioner at Poona, was murdered in 1897 by
option_1: Rash Behari Bose and Sachin Sanyal
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Chapekar brothers.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• W. C. Rand, the Special Plague Commissioner at Poona, was shot in 1897 by the Chapekar brothers, Damodar and Balkrishna, during the Viceroyalty of Lord Elgin II (1894-99) (चापेकर बंधु — रैंड की हत्या 1897)

 

• The brothers were angered by the harsh measures of the plague operations, including house searches and humiliation of residents.

 

• Lt. Ayerst was also killed, and the Chapekars were later hanged.

 

• Bal Gangadhar Tilak was prosecuted for sedition for his writings in the Kesari in connection with the episode.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Elgin II's term also saw the famine of 1896-97 and the Lyall Commission of 1898.

 

• The Chapekar brothers belonged to Poona and are reckoned among the first revolutionary terrorists.

 

• The Natu brothers were deported without trial in 1897.

 

• Tilak's Ganapati and Shivaji festivals encouraged nationalism in Maharashtra.

 

NOTE

 

• Rash Behari Bose and Sachin Sanyal (Option 1): Rash Behari Bose and Sachin Sanyal were associated with the Hardinge Bomb Conspiracy of 1912, the attempt to kill the Viceroy at Delhi, which came fifteen years after the Poona murder.

 

• Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki (Option 2): Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki threw a bomb at the carriage of Magistrate Kingsford at Muzaffarpur in 1908, which belongs to the Bengal revolutionary phase and not to Poona.

 

• Madan Lal Dhingra (Option 4): Madan Lal Dhingra shot Curzon Wyllie in London in 1909, an episode that took place abroad and well after the Rand murder of 1897 in Poona.

question:
Consider the following statements about Lord Curzon.

1. The Partition of Bengal took place in 1905 during his Viceroyalty.

2. He reorganised the Archaeological Survey of India in 1902.

3. The capital of British India was shifted from Calcutta to Delhi during his tenure.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Bengal was divided in 1905 into two provinces, a step that sparked the Swadeshi and Boycott movements (कर्जन — बंगाल विभाजन 1905)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: Curzon, an archaeologist by inclination, reorganised the Archaeological Survey of India in 1902, even though it had been founded in 1861 by Alexander Cunningham.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong because the capital was shifted from Calcutta to Delhi in 1911, announced at the Delhi Durbar during the time of Hardinge II.

 

• Curzon also appointed the Raleigh Commission on universities and enacted the Indian Universities Act of 1904.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Curzon resigned in 1905 after a dispute with Kitchener over the military department.

 

• The Ancient Monuments Preservation Act was passed in 1904.

 

• He formed the North-West Frontier Province in 1901.

 

• The Delhi Durbar of 1903 celebrated Edward VII's coronation.

 

• Curzon's Viceroyalty began in January 1899 and he was given a second term, but he quit in 1905 over his dispute with Kitchener.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 1): Going with 1 and 3 only drops the ASI reorganisation and adopts the false claim that Curzon shifted the capital, which took place in 1911 under Hardinge II.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): Choosing 2 and 3 only omits the Partition of Bengal, which is the best-known event of Curzon's tenure, and relies on the incorrect Delhi shift attribution.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Including all three statements is wrong because the transfer of the capital to Delhi was announced in 1911, after Curzon had resigned, and the other two statements alone describe his work.

question: Which of the following is NOT associated with the Viceroyalty of Lord Curzon?
option_4: Reorganisation of the Archaeological Survey of India, 1902
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vernacular Press Act, 1878.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 was passed under Lord Lytton to curb the Indian-language press, so it is not a Curzon measure (वर्नाक्यूलर प्रेस एक्ट — लिटन, 1878)

 

• The Indian Universities Act (1904) followed the Raleigh Commission and tightened official control over universities, under Curzon.

 

• The Partition of Bengal (1905) was carried out by Curzon on administrative grounds, with an underlying aim of dividing Bengali nationalism.

 

• The Archaeological Survey was reorganised in 1902 and John Marshall was appointed Director-General.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Lytton's Vernacular Press Act was repealed by Ripon in 1882.

 

• Curzon also passed the Official Secrets Act of 1904, restricting the press.

 

• The Calcutta Corporation Act of 1899 reduced the elected members.

 

• Curzon's police commission was headed by Andrew Fraser.

 

• Curzon described the Partition as an administrative step to ease the burden of the huge Bengal Presidency, which had about 78 million people.

 

NOTE

 

• Indian Universities Act, 1904 (Option 1): The Indian Universities Act of 1904 is a Curzon-era law enacted after the Raleigh Commission of 1902, so it is firmly connected with him and is not the exception sought by the question.

 

• Partition of Bengal, 1905 (Option 2): The Partition of Bengal was announced in July 1905 and effected in October of that year under Curzon, making it one of the best-known events of his Viceroyalty, not an exception.

 

• Reorganisation of the Archaeological Survey of India, 1902 (Option 4): The reorganisation of the Archaeological Survey in 1902 and the Ancient Monuments Act of 1904 reflect Curzon's interest in heritage, so this item is associated with him.

question: The capital of British India was transferred from Calcutta to Delhi in 1911 during the Viceroyalty of
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Hardinge II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The shift of the capital from Calcutta to Delhi was announced by George V at the Delhi Durbar of 1911 during the Viceroyalty of Lord Hardinge II (1910-16) (दिल्ली को राजधानी बनाया — हार्डिंग द्वितीय, 1911)

 

• The decision also annulled the Partition of Bengal of 1905, and Bengal was reunited with Bihar and Orissa separated as a new province.

 

• In 1912 the Hardinge Bomb Conspiracy, an attempt on the Viceroy's life at Delhi by Rash Behari Bose and Sachin Sanyal, took place during the entry procession.

 

• In 1915 Rabindranath Tagore was awarded a knighthood during his tenure, which he renounced after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The formal inauguration of New Delhi, designed by Lutyens and Baker, took place in 1931.

 

• Hardinge's period saw the beginning of the First World War.

 

• Minto II's term (1905-10) had the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909.

 

• Chelmsford succeeded Hardinge II in 1916.

 

• The Delhi Durbar of December 1911 was the occasion at which King George V and Queen Mary announced the change in person.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Minto II (Option 1): Lord Minto II (1905-10) is remembered for the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909, which introduced separate electorates; the capital was changed a year after he left office.

 

• Lord Chelmsford (Option 2): Lord Chelmsford (1916-21) came after the capital had already been shifted, and his name is attached to the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms of 1919 and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

 

• Lord Curzon (Option 3): Lord Curzon had left office in 1905, years before the Durbar of 1911, and in fact the Partition of Bengal that he carried out was reversed at the same time as the capital was shifted.

question:
Match the Viceroy in Column A with the event in Column B.

Column A: (a) Lord Minto II (b) Lord Reading (c) Lord Irwin (d) Lord Willingdon

Column B: (i) Communal Award (ii) First Round Table Conference (iii) Morley-Minto Reforms (iv) Introduction of ICS written examinations in India
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• (a) The Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 came under Lord Minto II (1905-10), so a-iii (वायसराय और घटनाएँ — सही मिलान)

 

• (b) Lord Reading (1921-26) saw the holding of written ICS examinations in India in 1922, so b-iv; the Chauri Chaura incident (1922) also occurred in his term.

 

• (c) The First Round Table Conference (1930) met in London while Lord Irwin (1926-31) was Viceroy, together with the Salt March and Civil Disobedience, so c-ii.

 

• (d) The Communal Award (1932) was announced under Lord Willingdon (1931-36), who also saw the second and third Round Table Conferences, so d-i.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Government of India Act 1935 was passed in Willingdon's period.

 

• Irwin announced the Dominion status goal in October 1929.

 

• The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed in March 1931.

 

• Morley-Minto Reforms gave separate electorates to Muslims.

 

• The Government of India Act 1909 popularly called the Morley-Minto Reforms enlarged the councils and allowed Indians to enter the Viceroy's Executive Council, with S. P. Sinha as the first.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i (Option 2): This combination swaps the Reading and Irwin events, putting the First Round Table Conference of 1930 under Reading and the ICS examinations in India under Irwin, which reverses both of them.

 

• a-i, b-iv, c-ii, d-iii (Option 3): This combination assigns the Communal Award to Minto II and the Morley-Minto Reforms to Willingdon, mixing a 1932 award with the 1909 reforms and misplacing both Viceroys.

 

• a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii (Option 4): This combination gives ICS written examinations to Minto II, Morley-Minto to Reading and the Communal Award to Irwin, so none of the Viceroys is matched with his own event.

question: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 13 April 1919 took place during the Viceroyalty of
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Chelmsford.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The massacre occurred in the term of Lord Chelmsford (1916-21), whose name is also linked to the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms of 1919 (जलियांवाला बाग हत्याकांड — चेम्सफोर्ड काल)

 

• On 10 April 1919, Mahatma Gandhi was arrested for the first time in India at Palwal Station while heading to Punjab, and three days later General Dyer fired on the crowd at Amritsar.

 

• The Rowlatt Act of 1919 had provoked the agitation that led to the events in Punjab.

 

• The Hunter Committee was appointed to inquire into the Punjab disturbances.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Government of India Act 1919 introduced dyarchy in the provinces.

 

• Chelmsford's period saw the beginning of the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1920.

 

• Reading succeeded Chelmsford in 1921.

 

• Tagore returned his knighthood after the massacre.

 

• General Reginald Dyer ordered the firing on a peaceful gathering assembled to protest against the Rowlatt Act and the arrest of Satyapal and Saifuddin Kitchlew.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Reading (Option 1): Lord Reading became Viceroy in 1921, after the massacre, and his term saw the Chauri Chaura incident and the withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922.

 

• Lord Hardinge II (Option 3): Lord Hardinge II left office in April 1916, nearly three years before the massacre, and is recalled instead for the capital shift of 1911 and the bomb attack of 1912.

 

• Lord Irwin (Option 4): Lord Irwin took over in 1926 and is associated with the Salt March of 1930 and the first Round Table Conference, so he was Viceroy long after the massacre.

question:
Consider the following statements about the later Viceroys.

1. The provincial elections under the Government of India Act 1935 were held in February 1937 during the term of Lord Linlithgow.

2. The Wavell Plan and the Shimla Conference took place during the term of Lord Wavell.

3. The June 3rd Plan was announced during the term of Lord Wavell.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the first elections to the Provincial Legislative Assemblies under the Government of India Act 1935 were held in February 1937 under Lord Linlithgow (1936-44) (लिनलिथगो और वेवल काल)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the Wavell Plan and the Shimla Conference (1945) belong to the period of Lord Wavell (1944-47), who tried to form an Executive Council with Indian members.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong because the June 3rd Plan (the Mountbatten Plan) was announced in 1947 by Lord Mountbatten, the last Viceroy.

 

• The Shimla Conference failed over the Muslim League's claim to nominate all Muslim members.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Congress formed ministries in seven provinces after the elections of 1937.

 

• Wavell was also Viceroy when the Cabinet Mission arrived in 1946.

 

• Linlithgow's term saw the outbreak of the Second World War and the August Offer of 1940.

 

• The Interim Government of 1946 was formed during Wavell's time.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 2): Selecting 1 and 3 only brings in the Mountbatten Plan as a Wavell act, but the plan of 3 June 1947 came after Wavell's replacement by Mountbatten in March 1947.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 3): Opting for 2 and 3 only overlooks the 1937 elections that happened under Linlithgow, and again attributes the June plan to Wavell, who was no longer in office in June 1947.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): All three cannot be right since the June 3rd Plan is the Mountbatten Plan of 1947; only the first two statements correctly describe developments under Linlithgow and Wavell.

question:
Consider the following statements.

1. Lord Mountbatten was the last Viceroy of India and the first Governor-General of independent India.

2. C. Rajagopalachari was the first Indian and the last Governor-General of India.

3. C. Rajagopalachari was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 1954.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Lord Mountbatten was the last Viceroy (March-August 1947) and then served as the first Governor-General of independent India until June 1948 (माउंटबेटन और राजगोपालाचारी)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: C. Rajagopalachari (June 1948 to January 1950) was the first Indian and also the last Governor-General of India, since the post ended when the Republic began on 26 January 1950.

 

• Statement 3 is correct: Rajagopalachari was among the first recipients of the Bharat Ratna in 1954, together with C. V. Raman and S. Radhakrishnan.

 

• All three statements agree with the record, making the full set the right choice.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rajagopalachari also served as Education Minister in the Interim Government and became Chief Minister of Madras in 1952.

 

• Dr Rajendra Prasad became the first President of India on 26 January 1950.

 

• Mountbatten had been Supreme Allied Commander in South East Asia.

 

• Rajagopalachari founded the Swatantra Party in 1959.

 

• Mountbatten returned home in June 1948, and the office of Governor-General was then given to Rajagopalachari until the adoption of the Constitution.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 2 only (Option 1): Going with 1 and 2 only omits the Bharat Ratna honour of 1954, which is a correct fact about Rajagopalachari, so it leaves out a statement that is accurate.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 3): Choosing 1 and 3 only leaves out the point that Rajagopalachari was the first Indian and last Governor-General, a position he held from 1948 until the Republic in 1950.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 4): Selecting 2 and 3 only excludes the first statement, but Mountbatten was indeed the last Viceroy and the first Governor-General of independent India after the transfer of power in 1947.

question:
Arrange the following Viceroys in chronological order of their tenure.

1. Lord Reading

2. Lord Hardinge II

3. Lord Willingdon

4. Lord Curzon
solution_text:
The correct answer is 4-2-1-3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lord Curzon (1899-1905) is the earliest of the four, with the Partition of Bengal in his term (वायसरायों का कालक्रम)

 

• Lord Hardinge II (1910-16) follows, with the shift of the capital to Delhi in 1911.

 

• Lord Reading (1921-26) comes next, with the Chauri Chaura incident of 1922.

 

• Lord Willingdon (1931-36) comes last, associated with the Communal Award and the Government of India Act 1935, so the right sequence is Curzon, Hardinge II, Reading, Willingdon.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Between Curzon and Hardinge II came Minto II (1905-10).

 

• Chelmsford governed between Hardinge II and Reading (1916-21).

 

• Irwin held the Viceroyalty in 1926-31, between Reading and Willingdon.

 

• Linlithgow followed Willingdon and held the longest Viceroyalty of the twentieth century, 1936-43/44.

 

• Willingdon's Viceroyalty also coincided with the Civil Disobedience movement's revival in 1932 and the Poona Pact, signed after Gandhi's fast.

 

NOTE

 

• 4-1-2-3 (Option 2): This order places Reading ahead of Hardinge II, but Hardinge II's term of 1910-16 ended five years before Reading took charge in 1921, so the middle pair is reversed.

 

• 2-4-1-3 (Option 3): This order puts Hardinge II ahead of Curzon, but Curzon's Viceroyalty ended in 1905 whereas Hardinge II took charge only in 1910, so the first two positions are interchanged in this sequence.

 

• 4-2-3-1 (Option 4): This order puts Willingdon before Reading, but Willingdon took office in 1931, ten years after Reading assumed the Viceroyalty in 1921, so the final two positions are interchanged.
